opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's both the most exciting and the most terrifying part of the job. When you're a student, you have an advisor who can catch you if a direction doesn't pan out, and you're often building on a vision that's already partly formed. Once you're leading the research yourself, there's no one telling you whether the problem is worth working on. You have to make that call, and you have to live with it for years.

What I've come to appreciate is that the hardest part isn't the technical work. It's choosing the problem. In robotics especially, there are a thousand interesting things you could do, and many of them are tractable but not very important, or important but not tractable yet. Finding the overlap, something that matters and that you can make real progress on with the resources you have, takes a kind of taste you only develop by making mistakes.

There's also a responsibility that comes with it. When I started my own lab, the decisions weren't just about my own career anymore. Students are betting several years of their lives on the directions I help set. That makes me more careful, but also more willing to commit. Hedging on everything doesn't really work, because the research that matters usually takes a sustained, focused push.

So how do I feel about it? I think I'd feel worse doing anything else. There's a freedom in being able to say, "I think this is how robots should learn, and I'm going to try to show it," even if you turn out to be wrong. That ownership is what makes the uncertainty worth it.

r001.rationale: The response describes leading research as exciting, says the freedom and ownership make the uncertainty worthwhile, and says she would feel worse doing anything else.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's a mix of exhilaration and a little bit of terror, and I think that's probably the healthy response.

When I was a PhD student, there was always this safety net. You have an advisor, you have senior labmates, and even when you're the one driving a project, somebody else has ultimately decided that this direction is worth betting on. You get to borrow their taste. The moment you become a faculty member and start your own group, that net is gone. Nobody is telling you what the important problems are anymore. You have to decide, and then you have to convince students to spend years of their lives on your bet. That part weighs on me more than the technical risk.

But I also think that's exactly where the fun is. In robot learning right now, there's so much that's genuinely unsettled. How much structure should we build into these systems versus how much should we let them learn from data? How do you get robots to do long-horizon tasks when the data you can collect is so limited compared to language or vision? These aren't questions where you can just follow the consensus, because there isn't one yet. So being forced to form my own opinion and then defend it with experiments is kind of the whole point.

The thing I've had to learn is that "leading it entirely yourself" is a bit of an illusion anyway. The best ideas in my group come out of arguments with students who think I'm wrong. My job is less about having all the answers and more about setting a direction that's worth arguing about, and then being honest enough to change course when the results tell me to. If I'm the only one with ideas, the lab isn't working.

So I'd say I've made peace with the uncertainty. I still get that pit in my stomach when I pick a new direction and don't know if it'll pan out. But I'd much rather have that feeling than be comfortably working on somebody else's agenda.

r001.rationale: She describes setting her own research direction as “exactly where the fun is” and says she would rather face that uncertainty than work on someone else’s agenda, conveying that leading research herself is especially gratifying.

astra-6.text: I think it’s both exciting and intimidating. When you’re leading the research yourself, you have the freedom to decide what questions matter, but you also have to take responsibility for that choice. There isn’t necessarily someone telling you, “This is the right direction.” You have to get comfortable with uncertainty and figure out what evidence would convince you to keep going—or change course. That’s challenging, but it’s also a part of research that I find really rewarding.

r001.rationale: She says that leading the research herself is challenging but also “really rewarding,” linking that reward to the freedom to choose research questions.
